paragraphs: A two-sample test asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. This matters both for scientific comparisons and for detecting changes in the data a machine-learning system encounters. The paper seeks to make these tests easier to use by connecting them to familiar supervised learning tools, reducing the need for specialized choices about testing procedures.

The method learns a witness function: a function whose average output can differ between the two samples. That difference becomes the test statistic. The central theoretical result shows that minimizing a squared loss leads to a witness with optimal testing power. This connection makes automated machine learning relevant: AutoML can supply the learning machinery for constructing the witness.

The authors apply the same automated method across a diverse distribution-shift benchmark and challenging testing problems, without user input specific to each problem. They report competitive performance. The finding supports a practical route to two-sample testing in which advances in automated prediction can also improve the construction of statistical tests.
neurips-2022-automl-two-sample-test-80ae.tldr: A squared-loss formulation lets AutoML learn powerful two-sample tests that perform competitively without problem-specific user input.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an image transmitted through a multi-mode optical fibre requires undoing the transformation into a speckle pattern. This paper builds a neural network around known angular correlations in those patterns. Its SO+(2,1)-equivariant construction also accounts for differences between the spatial arrangement of the original image and that of the measured speckle.

Reconstruction happens in two stages. The physically motivated network first predicts an image, and a separate network removes circular artifacts, fills gaps, and sharpens the result. Keeping these stages separate makes the first prediction available for inspection alongside the more polished output. The authors suggest that inspecting this intermediate result could be useful in safety-critical applications.

The architecture reduces the trainable parameter requirement from order N to the fourth power to order m, where N denotes pixel size and m the number of fibre modes. This supports demonstrated reconstruction at 256 by 256 pixels. The authors also report better generalization than previous models to images from classes absent during training, connecting the physical structure to both scalability and transfer.
neurips-2022-bessel-equivariant-networks.tldr: A physically structured equivariant network enables scalable fibre-image reconstruction, followed by a separate network for visual refinement.

paragraphs: Bandit learning involves repeatedly choosing among options while learning from the outcomes of those choices. Here, changing options also incurs a unit cost. The paper asks whether one algorithm can retain strong worst-case protection while exploiting the more favorable structure of a stochastically constrained setting. Regret measures the performance shortfall, including the cost of switching.

The proposed algorithm achieves regret of order T^(2/3), up to logarithmic factors, against an oblivious adversary. This matches the minimax rate at that level of precision. In the stochastically constrained regime, its bound becomes order min{log(T)/Δ², T^(2/3)}, where Δ is the gap between arms. This improves the previous order T^(1/3)/Δ guarantee stated in the abstract.

The paper also proves a complementary lower bound. Algorithms retaining the stated worst-case guarantee must, in general, incur stochastic-regime regret of at least order min{1/Δ², T^(2/3)}, ignoring logarithmic factors. Thus, the favorable-case improvement comes close to the unavoidable tradeoff imposed by preserving worst-case performance when switching is costly.
neurips-2022-better-best-of-both-worlds-.tldr: A simple bandit algorithm improves stochastic regret with switching costs while retaining near-optimal worst-case protection.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning trains representations by comparing related and unrelated views of graph data. The paper addresses two obstacles: manually designed graph transformations can require extensive trial and error, and existing methods can struggle when some node classes are much rarer than others. CM-GCL uses node content to construct comparisons automatically while seeking more balanced representations from unlabeled data.

For comparisons across modalities, the method pairs a node with content such as its text. It trains graph and content encoders to bring matching pairs closer and separate unrelated pairs. Network pruning helps identify minority nodes, motivated by the observation that pruning can cause minority examples to be forgotten. Two pruned encoders then learn together across the modalities.

Within the graph modality, a pruned and an unpruned graph encoder are co-trained to keep nodes with similar attributes close in representation space. The graph encoder is subsequently fine-tuned for imbalanced node classification. Experiments on real-world graphs report stronger performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods and more balanced representations.
neurips-2022-co-modality-graph-contrasti.tldr: CM-GCL combines graph-content comparisons and network pruning to learn more balanced representations for imbalanced node classification.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent can receive information through independent sampling, graph random walks, or other stochastic sequences. This paper studies how those input sequences affect the algorithm's long-run errors. It adapts efficiency ordering, a comparison tool from Markov Chain Monte Carlo, to compare the covariance matrices of appropriately scaled SGD errors.

The main result shows that sequences that are more efficient for MCMC sampling also yield smaller limiting error covariance for SGD. This ordering also implies smaller limiting mean squared error under arbitrary weighting. The result is relevant to decentralized optimization and swarm learning, where communication costs or privacy considerations can motivate moving through a network by random walk.

The framework shows that certain processes with memory can outperform Markovian alternatives, even when standard mixing-time analyses are difficult. Applications to shuffling and mini-batch gradient descent recover existing findings within one framework. Experiments also observe efficiency ordering for accelerated SGD and Adam, suggesting possible extensions; those observations are distinct from the paper's asymptotic SGD result.
neurips-2022-efficiency-ordering-of-stoc.tldr: An ordering borrowed from MCMC shows how more efficient sampling sequences reduce SGD's limiting error covariance.

paragraphs: Weakly supervised semantic segmentation needs useful estimates of where each object class appears without relying on full pixel-level supervision. Class activation maps provide such estimates, but often cover only part of an object or include incorrect regions. This paper separates improving coverage from removing mistakes through an expansion stage followed by a shrinkage stage.

Expansion uses learned sampling offsets in a deformable convolution layer. Its sampler is driven by an inverse supervision signal that maximizes the image-level classification loss, encouraging it to seek less discriminative object regions. The purpose is to extend localization beyond the most recognizable parts and recover a more complete object area.

The expanded region can also include background. A second deformable-convolution sampler therefore narrows it by excluding false positives, improving localization precision after expansion has improved recall. Experiments on PASCAL VOC 2012 and MS COCO 2014 report superiority over the compared state-of-the-art segmentation methods. The contribution is a sequential way to improve the pseudo ground truths on which weakly supervised segmentation depends.
neurips-2022-expansion-and-shrinkage-of-.tldr: Learned expansion and shrinkage samplers improve object coverage and remove background from weakly supervised localization maps.

paragraphs: A strictly 1-Lipschitz convolutional network limits how much its output can change relative to an input change measured in the l2 norm. Such constraints support adversarial robustness, interpretable gradients, and stable training. However, networks with provable constraints have often performed worse than approaches that enforce them only heuristically. This paper introduces three techniques to reduce that gap.

First, the authors replace the final linear layer with a multilayer perceptron containing one hidden layer and provide a robustness-certification procedure for this design. Second, they accelerate training of Skew Orthogonal Convolution layers. Third, they introduce pooling layers based on the fact that distance to a manifold is a 1-Lipschitz function.

The methods improve both ordinary accuracy and provably robust accuracy. Reported gains are 1.79 and 3.82 percentage points on CIFAR-10, and 3.78 and 4.75 on CIFAR-100, respectively. Training time per epoch for deeper networks using the SOC improvement falls by more than 30%. Together, these results address prediction quality, certification, and computational cost within the constrained-network setting.
neurips-2022-improved-techniques-for-det.tldr: New output layers, pooling constructions, and faster orthogonal convolutions improve accuracy and certified l2 robustness.

paragraphs: Mutual information measures dependence between random variables, but estimating it in high dimensions can be difficult. Sliced mutual information addresses this by averaging dependence measurements across one-dimensional random projections. This paper studies the broader k-sliced version, which projects into k-dimensional subspaces, to quantify how projection size, original dimension, and sample count interact.

The analysis uses a new continuity result for differential entropy under the 2-Wasserstein metric. From it, the authors derive sharp error bounds for Monte Carlo estimates with explicit dependence on both dimensions. They also combine Monte Carlo integration with neural estimation, producing an end-to-end estimator for which they establish optimal convergence rates.

The paper additionally examines how the population dependence measure behaves as dimension grows. Gaussian approximations have residual errors that decay under appropriate moment bounds, so this conclusion depends on those conditions. Numerical experiments and an application to sliced InfoGAN support the theory. Setting k to one recovers ordinary sliced mutual information, making the analysis directly relevant to its scalability.
neurips-2022-k-sliced-mutual-information.tldr: The paper quantifies how projection dimension, ambient dimension, and sample size govern k-sliced mutual-information estimation.

paragraphs: An individualized treatment rule selects a treatment using a patient's characteristics. Learning such a rule becomes challenging when many treatments are available, especially when some treatments may have similar effects. This paper proposes learning which treatments belong together while simultaneously estimating the treatment rule, allowing the grouping to inform the decision problem.

The method uses adaptive fusion in a single convex optimization problem. A loss term measures fit, while a penalty encourages similar treatments to merge into groups. Varying the tuning parameter produces a hierarchy that makes the treatment-clustering path visible. An accelerated proximal-gradient algorithm handles computation, and a group-lasso procedure selects variables to further improve performance.

The authors provide a theoretical guarantee for recovering the underlying treatment groups. Simulations and a cancer-treatment data application show superior performance in the reported evaluations. The practical contribution is a joint approach to simplifying a large treatment space and learning personalized choices, with a hierarchical representation that may help doctors understand the resulting treatment organization.
neurips-2022-learning-individualized-tre.tldr: Adaptive fusion jointly groups treatments with similar effects and learns individualized treatment rules through convex optimization.

paragraphs: Assigning multiple robots or machines to tasks becomes difficult when rewards depend on timing and assignments interact. The paper studies this through the multi-robot reward collection problem, which models settings such as ride-sharing and pickup-and-delivery. Its aim is to learn near-optimal planning behavior for this NP-hard problem class.

The authors formulate planning as sequential decision making and represent each state using an extension of probabilistic graphical models called random PGMs. They develop a mean-field inference method for these representations. Building on this, they introduce an order-transferable estimator of action values and an auction that uses this property to select a joint assignment in polynomial time.

These components form a reinforcement-learning framework with a stated optimality guarantee of at least 1−1/e. Experiments on reward-collection problems support the methods' near-optimality and transferability. The paper also considers identical parallel machine scheduling and minimax multiple traveling-salesman problems. The contribution combines structured inference, learned action evaluation, and efficient assignment selection for the planning settings studied.
neurips-2022-learning-np-hard-multi-agen.tldr: Structured graph inference and an auction-based assignment mechanism support learned multi-agent planning with a stated approximation guarantee.

paragraphs: Generating data that satisfies several conditions usually requires training examples annotated with multiple labels. Those annotations can be expensive. This paper considers a more limited setting: each example has one known positive label, and there are no explicit negative labels. An absent annotation therefore does not establish that a condition is absent from the example.

The proposed single-to-multi-label sampling method, S2M, uses Markov chain Monte Carlo to draw samples satisfying multiple labels. It operates as an add-on to existing generative adversarial networks, including both unconditional and conditional GANs. This makes the sampling procedure the central mechanism for obtaining multi-label outputs from the single-positive setting.

Experiments on real image datasets support the method's effectiveness and correctness, including comparisons with a model trained using fully annotated data. The findings suggest that useful control over several output conditions can be obtained with substantially lighter annotation requirements. The paper's contribution is specifically a broadly applicable sampling approach that enables existing GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data.
neurips-2022-mining-multi-label-samples-.tldr: S2M uses MCMC sampling to obtain multi-label GAN outputs from data annotated with only one positive label per example.

paragraphs: In decentralized learning, participants exchange messages with neighbors rather than exposing everything to a central observer. The paper asks how to quantify the privacy benefit of that limited visibility. It introduces pairwise network differential privacy, a relaxation of local differential privacy in which leakage from one participant to another can depend on their relative graph positions.

The analysis combines locally added noise with gossip averaging, where information is exchanged and averaged across the network. It covers simple and randomized gossip on fixed and random communication graphs. The authors also construct a private decentralized optimization algorithm that alternates local gradient-descent updates with gossip averaging.

The resulting privacy amplification depends on distance between nodes. The privacy-utility tradeoff matches that of a trusted curator up to explicit graph-topology factors; for expander graphs, those factors become constant. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data illustrate the gains. The contribution makes network structure part of the privacy analysis, capturing distinctions that ordinary local guarantees overlook.
neurips-2022-muffliato-peer-to-peer-priv.tldr: Muffliato quantifies how network position and gossip communication amplify privacy in decentralized averaging and optimization.

paragraphs: Deep-learning models in neuroscience are sometimes interpreted as explanations of brain circuits, including what those circuits optimize. This paper examines that interpretation through models of grid cells in the entorhinal-hippocampal circuit. It asks whether the models deliver new neural predictions or reveal fundamental functions, rather than merely producing a familiar-looking result.

The authors first review insights from first-principles modeling, then investigate deep-learning claims using broad architecture and hyperparameter sweeps alongside theory-driven experiments. Their results show that model behavior may depend more strongly on particular implementation choices, including post-hoc choices, than on fundamental properties of neural circuits or the proposed learning objectives.

The paper argues that accurate brain models require substantial inductive bias informed by biology, framing this as an informal no-free-lunch result. It also proposes hypotheses about additional loss functions that could make grid cells emerge more robustly. The implication is a call for transparent implementation choices and biological grounding when interpreting learned representations as scientific evidence about neural mechanisms.
neurips-2022-no-free-lunch-from-deep-lea.tldr: A grid-cell case study shows that implementation choices can drive neural-model results, complicating claims about brain function.

paragraphs: Controlled feature selection seeks relevant variables while keeping the false discovery rate below a chosen level. The paper identifies two reasons existing deep-learning approaches based on Model-X knockoffs can fail: inaccurate models of the feature distribution and insufficient enforcement of the swap property required for valid knockoffs. FlowSelect takes a different route to statistical testing.

FlowSelect models the feature distribution with normalizing flows and uses an MCMC procedure to calculate a p-value for each feature directly. This avoids having to enforce the knockoff swap property. The theoretical validity statement is asymptotic: the procedure computes valid p-values in the limit, rather than establishing an unconditional finite-sample guarantee in the abstract.

On synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks, FlowSelect consistently controls the false discovery rate and has greater power, while the compared knockoff approaches fail to maintain control. An application to soybean association data also identifies genetic variants linked to specific traits. The results support combining density estimation with direct testing as an effective alternative to learned knockoff construction.
neurips-2022-normalizing-flows-for-knock.tldr: FlowSelect combines normalizing flows and MCMC-based p-values to select features with asymptotic validity and empirical false-discovery control.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds describe how far a model's performance on training data can differ from its performance on the underlying population. Many existing techniques require strong restrictions, such as a loss that is uniformly bounded or Lipschitz. This paper develops a bound using average restrictions on the loss and its gradient norm instead.

The derivation exploits the contractivity of log-Sobolev inequalities. This introduces an additional term involving the loss-gradient norm into the generalization bound. Intuitively, that term acts as a surrogate for model complexity: the analysis makes gradient magnitude an explicit part of how generalization is assessed. The assumptions are relaxed from uniform control to on-average control, so the result still relies on boundedness conditions of the latter kind.

The authors apply the bound to Bayesian deep neural networks and empirically examine the gradient-norm term across different architectures. The contribution therefore includes both a theoretical route under weaker forms of boundedness and an investigation of how the new term behaves in neural-network applications.
neurips-2022-on-the-importance-of-gradie.tldr: A new generalization bound replaces uniform restrictions with average loss and gradient-norm assumptions and explicitly incorporates gradient magnitude.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned environment model to generate experience for policy improvement. As the policy changes, the states it visits also change, making accurate modeling difficult. The paper highlights two problems: uncertainty is often measured only after samples are generated, and models trained for one-step prediction are used to produce multi-step trajectories.

Plan To Predict treats trajectory generation itself as sequential decision making. It reverses the usual perspective by making the model the decision maker and treating the current policy as the dynamics. This lets the model adapt to the policy and anticipate uncertainty several steps ahead while generating trajectories, addressing the mismatch between model training and use.

The theoretical analysis connects P2P's performance guarantee to approximately optimizing a lower bound on return in the true environment. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on several challenging benchmarks. The central idea is to train prediction with future trajectory quality in view, so model-generated experience reflects uncertainty that may arise beyond the next step.
neurips-2022-plan-to-predict-learning-an.tldr: P2P trains an environment model to anticipate multi-step uncertainty by treating trajectory generation as a decision problem.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn a useful policy from logged data without gathering more experience from the environment. A learned environment model can support policy optimization, but behavior outside the dataset's coverage needs conservative treatment. RAMBO addresses this by making the model an adversary that challenges the policy's estimated performance.

The formulation is a two-player zero-sum game. The policy seeks higher value, while the environment model is trained to lower that value subject to accurately predicting transitions in the dataset. This creates pressure for conservative behavior in poorly covered regions. The method approximately solves the game by alternating policy optimization with adversarial model optimization.

The formulation has a probably approximately correct performance guarantee and a pessimistic value function that lower-bounds value in the true environment. Evaluations on widely studied offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks report improvements over existing state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution is to build conservatism into the interaction between policy and model while keeping the adversarial model anchored to observed transitions.
neurips-2022-rambo-rl-robust-adversarial.tldr: RAMBO learns conservative offline policies by alternating policy improvement with an adversarial environment model constrained by logged transitions.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph completion predicts missing relationships between entities. Factorization models such as DistMult have performed strongly on this task, often outperforming graph neural networks. However, they struggle to incorporate node features and handle previously unseen nodes. ReFactor GNNs aim to combine the predictive strengths of factorization with the inductive capabilities of graph neural networks.

The key connection comes from viewing optimization as message passing. The authors reformulate gradient-descent updates in factorization models as operations that exchange information across the graph. This shows how factorization models can be expressed through a GNN formalism and provides the basis for the new architecture, linking two approaches previously regarded as largely separate.

Across established knowledge graph completion benchmarks, ReFactor GNNs match factorization models' transductive performance and achieve state-of-the-art inductive performance with an order of magnitude fewer parameters. These results suggest that the message-passing interpretation can preserve strong predictions for known entities while supporting generalization to unseen ones in a more compact model.
neurips-2022-refactor-gnns-revisiting-fa.tldr: ReFactor GNNs reinterpret factorization-model optimization as message passing to combine strong graph completion with unseen-node generalization.

paragraphs: Many statistical and econometric models identify an unknown parameter through moment conditions, which specify relationships among expected quantities. Generalized Method of Moments is a standard way to solve those conditions, but outliers can strongly distort its estimates. Earlier robust versions face problems involving computational cost, dimensional scaling, or missing quantitative guarantees under substantial contamination.

The paper develops a computationally efficient estimator that, under its stated assumptions, tolerates a constant fraction ε of adversarially corrupted observations. Its parameter-recovery error in Euclidean distance is of order √ε. The construction extends techniques from algorithmic robust statistics previously used for simpler tasks such as mean estimation, linear regression, and stochastic optimization.

As a concrete application, the authors study instrumental-variables linear regression with heterogeneous treatment effects. Experiments show tolerance of corruption levels as high as 10–15%, substantially improving on the compared baselines. The contribution joins an explicit contamination-dependent recovery guarantee with efficient computation, while the experimental application demonstrates robustness in one particular inference setting.
neurips-2022-robust-generalized-method-o.tldr: A computationally efficient robust GMM estimator tolerates adversarial contamination with an assumption-dependent error guarantee of order √ε.

paragraphs: The paper studies a sender who reveals information to influence a self-interested receiver making sequential decisions. The sender observes random events but initially does not know their probabilities, so learning and persuasion must happen together. The goal is to obtain low regret for the sender while making recommendations worthwhile for the receiver.

The authors construct a tractable geometric approximation of persuasive information structures, then prove that exact persuasiveness cannot be guaranteed by a learning algorithm in this setting. They therefore relax the requirement: the receiver's regret from following recommendations should grow sublinearly. With full feedback about all random-event realizations, they obtain roughly square-root-in-T regret for both parties, ignoring logarithmic factors.

With bandit feedback, the sender sees only events actually encountered. A parameter α between one-half and one gives sender regret of order T^α and receiver regret of order T^max{α,1−α/2}, again hiding logarithmic factors. A lower bound shows this tradeoff is essentially tight. Thus, limited observation imposes a quantified tension between the two parties' learning guarantees.
neurips-2022-sequential-information-desi.tldr: Learning to persuade under unknown event probabilities requires relaxed incentives, with sharp regret tradeoffs under limited feedback.

paragraphs: Nonconvex optimization can be difficult even when only noisy gradient information is available. This paper studies objectives with a global Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz inequality, a structural condition that makes global optimization analysis possible. It also assumes a mild expected-smoothness property for the stochastic gradient queries and develops a framework for analyzing SGD's nonlinear dynamics.

For objectives satisfying the α-PL condition, the analysis gives SGD a sample complexity of order ε^−((4−α)/α), where ε is the target accuracy and α describes gradient domination. This quantifies how the objective's structure affects the amount of stochastic information needed. The guarantee concerns this structured class of nonconvex objectives.

The authors then introduce PAGER, a modified SGD method combining variance reduction and restarting. Under an average-smoothness assumption, its sample complexity improves to order ε^(−2/α). For α equal to one, the paper establishes the first optimal algorithm for that case, which occurs in applications including reinforcement-learning policy optimization. The improved rate is therefore tied to the stated objective and smoothness assumptions.
neurips-2022-sharp-analysis-of-stochasti.tldr: Under global KL-related conditions, variance reduction and restarting improve stochastic optimization rates and achieve optimality for α=1.

paragraphs: Sparse regression often starts with many candidate predictors while seeking a model that uses relatively few. Screening rules speed up fitting by discarding predictors beforehand. This paper introduces the Hessian Screening Rule for computing the lasso path, the sequence of solutions obtained as the strength of regularization changes.

The rule uses second-order information from the model, which describes curvature rather than only the direction of local change. That information supports both effective predictor screening and accurate warm starts for subsequent optimization problems. The authors emphasize screening effectiveness when predictors are highly correlated, a setting where relationships among predictors are particularly relevant to deciding what to retain.

In simulations with both low and high correlation, the proposed rule outperforms every alternative studied for l1-regularized least-squares and logistic regression. It also generally performs best on the real datasets examined. The findings support curvature information as a practical way to accelerate sparse-model fitting across a regularization path, with empirical advantages in both correlated and less-correlated settings.
neurips-2022-the-hessian-screening-rule-.tldr: The Hessian Screening Rule uses model curvature to discard predictors and improve warm starts when fitting sparse regression paths.

paragraphs: Weak supervision trains classifiers using imperfect labeling signals, often taking every example those signals cover. This paper shows theoretically and empirically that using all such data is not always optimal. More examples provide more training information, but inaccurate weak labels can reduce the value of that additional data.

The proposed method combines pretrained representations with a cut statistic to select a subset intended to have higher-quality weak labels. It makes the tradeoff between data quantity and label precision an explicit part of the training pipeline. The selection step can be used with any label model and classifier, and the authors describe it as requiring only a few lines of integration code.

Evaluations span a wide range of label models, classifiers, and datasets. Selecting fewer weakly labeled examples improves accuracy by as much as 19 percentage points on benchmark tasks. That maximum is an observed result across the evaluations. The broader finding is that choosing training examples can be a useful component of weak supervision alongside constructing and combining labeling signals.
neurips-2022-training-subset-selection-f.tldr: Selecting higher-quality subsets of weakly labeled data can improve accuracy, with reported gains of up to 19 percentage points.

paragraphs: Incremental implicitly refined classification requires assigning hierarchical labels as learning proceeds through successive phases. New classes can be refinements of previously learned ones, so the representation must accommodate more detail while preserving relevant relationships. The paper identifies a weakness in existing methods: their descriptors can become inconsistent when new classes inherit from old classes.

Uncertainty-Aware Hierarchical Refinement addresses this with two strategies. Global representation extension widens the relevant margins to make incremental representations more discriminative. Hierarchical distribution alignment explicitly identifies class inheritance relationships and uses them to refine distillation, the process of transferring learned information. Hierarchical uncertainty also guides corrections to shifting subclasses so that similar features remain consistent.

Experiments on IIRC-CIFAR and three IIRC-ImageNet variants report improvements over state-of-the-art approaches. The result supports treating the class hierarchy as an active part of incremental learning: representation separation, knowledge transfer, and subclass correction all account for how labels become more specific. This targets the particular difficulty of learning refinements while retaining coherence across levels of the hierarchy.
neurips-2022-uncertainty-aware-hierarchi.tldr: UAHR uses class inheritance and hierarchical uncertainty to keep representations consistent as incremental labels become more specific.

paragraphs: An intervention can leave the average outcome unchanged while helping some people and harming others. Observed data cannot reveal both outcomes for the same person, so the fraction harmed generally cannot be identified exactly. This paper focuses on bounding that fraction as tightly as the available factual observations permit.

The authors derive sharp bounds for the fraction negatively affected and related quantities using experimental or observational data. Stratifying people by observable characteristics tightens the bounds by incorporating more information about outcome differences across groups. This approach preserves the uncertainty created by missing counterfactuals while extracting the strongest supported range for the population impact.

Because the bounds depend on functions estimated from data, the paper develops a robust inference algorithm. It remains efficient across broad choices and rates of function learning, consistent when some functions are mislearned, and conservatively valid when most are mislearned. Simulations and a career-counseling case study illustrate the method. The contribution supports credible conclusions about possible harm without claiming to recover unobservable individual effects exactly.
neurips-2022-what-s-the-harm-sharp-bound.tldr: Sharp bounds and robust inference quantify how many people an intervention may harm despite unobserved counterfactual outcomes.
